title: Tensor product with a constant complex
statement:
Let $X$ be a
quasi-compact and
quasi-separated scheme with $\kuncd(X)<\infty$ and let $\Lambda$ be
a torsion ring. For $E\in D(X_{\Et},\Lambda)$ and
$K\in D(\Lambda)$, the canonical map

$$
\RGamma(X_{\Et},E)\kunotimes{\Lambda}K\longrightarrow
\RGamma\bigl(X_{\Et},E\kunotimes{\Lambda}\underline{K}\bigr)
$$

is an isomorphism.

proof.text: Write $\mathcal A=\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\Et},\Lambda)$ and $\Gamma=\Gamma(X,-):\mathcal A\to\operatorname{Mod}(\Lambda)$. The category $\mathcal A$ is Grothendieck abelian. Sections are additive and preserve kernels, so $\Gamma$ is left exact. Put $d=\kuncd(X)<\infty$. A torsion unital ring has some integer $n\ge1$ with $n1=0$, hence every $\Lambda$-module sheaf is a torsion abelian sheaf. The coefficient-forgetting cohomology comparison therefore gives $R^q\Gamma(M)=0$ for all $M\in\mathcal A$ and $q>d$. For any set-indexed family $(M_i)$, its sum is the filtered colimit of its finite subsums, in both module sheaves and underlying abelian sheaves. Finite sums of injective resolutions are injective resolutions (extend a map into each coordinate separately), and additivity gives $R^q\Gamma(\bigoplus_{i\in J}M_i)=\bigoplus_{i\in J}R^q\Gamma(M_i)$ for finite $J$. Cohomology commutes with this filtered colimit on the qcqs scheme $X$, including constant-ring module coefficients. Thus the canonical map $\bigoplus_iR^q\Gamma(M_i)\to R^q\Gamma(\bigoplus_iM_i)$ is an isomorphism for every $q\ge0$. This proves the sheaf-level input of Stacks 0F11 for the actual ring $\Lambda$, rather than assuming its stated $\mathbf Z/n$ conclusion also covers $\Lambda$.

For an arbitrary family $(E_i)$ in $D(\mathcal A)$ choose K-injective representatives $I_i^\bullet$ with injective terms. The termwise sum $J^\bullet=\bigoplus_i I_i^\bullet$ represents $\bigoplus_iE_i$. Each injective term is $\Gamma$-acyclic: the resolution concentrated in degree zero computes its higher derived sections as zero. Step 1 gives $R^q\Gamma(J^r)=\bigoplus_i R^q\Gamma(I_i^r)=0$ for $q>0$. The unbounded acyclic-complex theorem applies, with the uniform bound $d$, and computes $R\Gamma(E_i)$ and $R\Gamma(\bigoplus_iE_i)$ by $\Gamma(I_i^\bullet)$ and $\Gamma(J^\bullet)$ respectively, naturally on all coprojections. The $q=0$ comparison of Step 1 gives a termwise isomorphism $\theta^r:\bigoplus_i\Gamma(I_i^r)\to\Gamma(J^r)$. Since $d_J\iota_i=\iota_i d_{I_i}$, equality on every coprojection gives $\Gamma(d_J)\theta^r=\theta^{r+1}(\bigoplus_i\Gamma(d_{I_i}))$. Thus $\theta$ is a complex isomorphism preserving coprojections. Termwise sums compute coproducts in $D(\Lambda)$, proving that the canonical comparison $\bigoplus_iR\Gamma(E_i)\to R\Gamma(\bigoplus_iE_i)$ is invertible. No assertion that $J^\bullet$ is K-injective is needed.

Let $a:(\operatorname{Sh}(X_{\Et}),\Lambda_X)\to(\operatorname{Sets},\Lambda)$ be the terminal geometric morphism, presented using the small etale site and the one-object point site. Its module inverse image is the constant-sheaf functor: a presheaf map from the constant presheaf $M$ to a sheaf $F$ is determined by its component $M\to F(X)$ at the terminal object, and conversely restriction of that component defines every component on $U\to X$. For the constant presheaf of rings $\mathcal O(U)=\Lambda$, the component maps are $\Lambda$-linear. The module-sheafification interface, applied to this presheaf ring and the constant presheaf module $M$, extends its action to $\mathcal O^\#=\Lambda_X$ and identifies $\Lambda_X$-linear maps $\underline M\to F$ with these presheaf $\Lambda$-linear maps, hence with module maps $M\to\Gamma(X,F)$, and its coefficient ring map is the identity $a^{-1}\Lambda=\Lambda_X$. The constant-complex construction preserves quasi-isomorphisms, so $La^*K=\underline K$. The derived ringed-topos adjunction identifies $Ra_*$ with $R\Gamma$. Apply the ringed projection-mate statement to this morphism and the fixed $E$. It supplies exact functors $F(K)=R\Gamma(E)\otimes^L_\Lambda K$ and $G(K)=R\Gamma(E\otimes^L_\Lambda La^*K)$ and a natural transformation $\alpha:F\to G$, compatible with shifts and distinguished triangles. Its component is adjoint to $(\varepsilon_E\otimes1)\mu_{R\Gamma(E),K}$, hence is exactly the canonical map in the item, including its connecting-square compatibility.

proof.text: The functor $F$ preserves set-indexed coproducts. Here is the module-complex argument, so that no etale-sheaf tensor lemma is misapplied to $D(\Lambda)$. On the point site choose K-flat flat-term models $P$ of $R\Gamma(E)$ and $C_i$ of $K_i$. The canonical distribution map $\operatorname{Tot}(P\otimes\bigoplus_i C_i)\cong\bigoplus_i\operatorname{Tot}(P\otimes C_i)$ sends $p\otimes(c_i)_i$ to $(p\otimes c_i)_i$ on finite-support tensors; its inverse uses the coprojections. Both maps respect $d_P\otimes1+(-1)^p1\otimes d_C$. For an acyclic complex $B$, the degree-$n$ distribution isomorphism is $\bigoplus_{p+q=n}B^p\otimes(\bigoplus_i C_i^q)\cong\bigoplus_i\bigoplus_{p+q=n}B^p\otimes C_i^q$, with the displayed signed differentials. Thus $\operatorname{Tot}(B\otimes(\bigoplus_i C_i))$ is the sum of the acyclic $\operatorname{Tot}(B\otimes C_i)$, whose cycles and boundaries are respectively the sums of cycles and boundaries. The terms of $\bigoplus_i C_i$ are flat, since tensoring a module short exact sequence with a sum is the sum of the exact tensor sequences. The derived-tensor descent statement now computes both sides by these total complexes. Termwise module sums compute derived coproducts, so the displayed isomorphism localizes to the canonical coproduct comparison for $F$. This also includes the empty family.

The functor $G$ preserves set-indexed coproducts as well. The derived adjunction of Step 3 makes $L=La^*$ a left adjoint to $R=R\Gamma$. Explicitly $\operatorname{Hom}(L(\bigoplus_iK_i),H)=\operatorname{Hom}(\bigoplus_iK_i,RH)=\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(K_i,RH)=\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(LK_i,H)$, naturally in $H$, and the bijections take the legs to $L$ of the original coprojections. This is the coproduct universal property, so $L$ preserves these sums. Tensor with $E$ in the etale derived category preserves sums by the cited tensor theorem. Applying the coproduct comparison for $R\Gamma$ proved in Step 2 proves the assertion for their composite $G$. Under the two functors' coproduct comparisons, naturality on each coprojection identifies $\alpha_{\bigoplus_iK_i}$ with $\bigoplus_i\alpha_{K_i}$. Thus if every $\alpha_{K_i}$ is invertible, the direct sum of their inverses is an inverse of this component.

Let $\mathcal C$ be the full subcategory of $D(\Lambda)$ consisting of $K$ for which $\alpha_K$ is invertible. Under the tensor-unit identifications the projection mate satisfies $\alpha_\Lambda=1_{R\Gamma(E)}$. Its compatibility with integer shifts identifies $\alpha_{\Lambda[k]}$ with the shift of that identity, so $\Lambda[k]\in\mathcal C$ for every integer $k$.

For a distinguished triangle in $D(\Lambda)$, Step 3 produces a morphism between its images under $F$ and $G$, including the shifted connecting square. The third-isomorphism triangle theorem shows that if two vertices lie in $\mathcal C$, then the third does too. The class is also closed under isomorphisms by naturality and under retracts: if $i:K\to H$, $r:H\to K$ satisfy $ri=1$ and $\alpha_H$ is invertible, then $F(r)\alpha_H^{-1}G(i):G(K)\to F(K)$ is inverse to $\alpha_K$. Indeed naturality gives $\alpha_K F(r)=G(r)\alpha_H$ and $G(i)\alpha_K=\alpha_H F(i)$, so the two composites reduce to $G(ri)$ and $F(ri)$. Together with Steps 4-5 this proves all required closure properties.

Apply derived-module free generation with $A=\Lambda$. The subcategory $\mathcal C$ contains all shifts $\Lambda[k]$ by Step 6 and is closed under set-indexed direct sums, third vertices of distinguished triangles, and retracts by Steps 5 and 7. It therefore contains every object of $D(\Lambda)$. Hence $\alpha_K$ is invertible for the arbitrary complex $K$ in the statement. This is precisely the canonical tensor-with-constant-complex map identified in Step 3.
